Scenario: A single mother lived with her 10-year-old son for the entire year and paid all costs of keeping up their home. What filing status should she use?
Choice1: Single
Choice2: Head of Household
Choice3: Qualifying Surviving Spouse
Explanation: Head of Household requires an unmarried taxpayer who pays more than half the cost of keeping up a home for a qualifying person, like her son, for more than half the year.

Scenario: Divorced parents cannot agree on who claims their child. The child lived with the mother for 220 nights and the father for 145 nights during the year, and no Form 8332 was signed. Who is entitled to claim the child?
Choice1: The father, because he requests it first
Choice2: The mother, because the child lived with her more of the year
Choice3: Either parent, split 50/50
Explanation: Without a signed Form 8332 release, the custodial parent - the one the child lived with for more nights during the year - is entitled to claim the child as a dependent.

Scenario: A 20-year-old is a full-time college student who earned $3,000 from a part-time job. Her parents provide more than half of her support. Can she still be claimed as their dependent?
Choice1: No, because she has her own income
Choice2: No, because she is over 18
Choice3: Yes, a full-time student under 24 can still qualify if the support test is met
Explanation: A qualifying child can be up to age 23 if they are a full-time student, as long as the parents still provide more than half of their support.

Scenario: A taxpayer sold stock they had owned for 8 months at a gain. How is that gain taxed?
Choice1: As a long-term capital gain
Choice2: As a short-term capital gain, taxed at ordinary rates
Choice3: It is not taxable
Explanation: Assets held one year or less produce short-term capital gains, which are taxed the same as ordinary income rather than at the lower long-term rates.

Scenario: A taxpayer received a Form 1099-G showing $2,400 in unemployment compensation. How should this be reported?
Choice1: It is not taxable and does not need to be reported
Choice2: It is fully taxable income reported on Schedule 1
Choice3: It is taxable only if the taxpayer also had wage income
Explanation: Unemployment compensation is fully taxable at the federal level and is reported as income on Schedule 1, which flows to Form 1040.

Scenario: A taxpayer won $1,500 at a casino but did not receive a Form W-2G. Do they still need to report the winnings?
Choice1: No, only winnings reported on a W-2G are taxable
Choice2: Yes, all gambling winnings are taxable regardless of whether a form was issued
Choice3: Only if the winnings exceed $5,000
Explanation: Gambling winnings are fully taxable as other income whether or not a Form W-2G was issued for the amount won.

Scenario: A 45-year-old withdraws $10,000 from her traditional IRA to pay for a vacation. What is the likely tax consequence?
Choice1: No tax consequence, since it is her own money
Choice2: The withdrawal is taxable income and likely subject to a 10% additional tax
Choice3: The withdrawal is tax-free but subject to a penalty only
Explanation: A traditional IRA withdrawal before age 59 and a half is included in taxable income and generally triggers a 10% additional tax unless an exception applies, and a vacation is not an exception.

Scenario: A taxpayer moves her entire 401(k) balance directly into a traditional IRA through a trustee-to-trustee transfer. What is the tax result?
Choice1: Fully taxable in the year of the rollover
Choice2: No tax consequence, since it is a direct, properly completed rollover
Choice3: Subject to the 10% early withdrawal penalty
Explanation: A direct trustee-to-trustee rollover between qualified retirement accounts is not taxable and does not trigger the early withdrawal penalty.

Scenario: A taxpayer contributed to a Roth IRA and later withdraws only her original contributions, not earnings, at age 40. Is this withdrawal taxable?
Choice1: Yes, all Roth withdrawals before 59 and a half are taxable
Choice2: No, contributions can be withdrawn tax-free and penalty-free at any time
Choice3: Only half of it is taxable
Explanation: Because Roth contributions were already taxed before going in, the contribution portion can always be withdrawn tax-free and penalty-free, regardless of age.

Scenario: A taxpayer turned 50 this year and wants to maximize her traditional IRA contribution. What applies?
Choice1: She can only contribute the standard limit; catch-up contributions start at 55
Choice2: She is now eligible for an additional catch-up contribution on top of the standard limit
Choice3: Turning 50 has no effect on IRA contribution limits
Explanation: Taxpayers age 50 and older are allowed an additional catch-up contribution to IRAs each year, on top of the standard contribution limit.

Scenario: A self-employed taxpayer pays $6,000 in self-employment tax for the year. How much of that can he deduct as an adjustment to income?
Choice2: One-half of the self-employment tax
Choice3: None of it is deductible
Explanation: Self-employed taxpayers can deduct one-half of their self-employment tax as an adjustment to income on Schedule 1.

Scenario: A taxpayer contributes $2,000 directly to her HSA outside of any payroll deduction. Where does this benefit show up on her return?
Choice1: As an itemized deduction on Schedule A
Choice2: As an adjustment to income on Schedule 1
Choice3: As a tax credit
Explanation: HSA contributions made outside of payroll are deducted as an adjustment to income, reducing AGI even if the taxpayer doesn't itemize.

Scenario: A taxpayer age 40 withdraws HSA funds to pay for a family vacation. What is the tax consequence?
Choice1: Tax-free, since it is her own HSA
Choice2: The withdrawal is taxable income and generally hit with a 20% additional tax
Choice3: Only the earnings portion is taxed
Explanation: HSA withdrawals for non-qualified expenses before age 65 are taxable income and generally subject to an additional 20% tax.

Scenario: A 67-year-old withdraws HSA funds to pay for home repairs, not a medical expense. What happens?
Choice1: The withdrawal is taxed as ordinary income but avoids the 20% additional tax because she is over 65
Choice2: The withdrawal is completely tax-free because she is over 65
Choice3: The withdrawal is subject to both income tax and the 20% additional tax
Explanation: After age 65, non-medical HSA withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income but no longer trigger the 20% additional tax.

Scenario: A taxpayer's total itemized deductions come to less than the standard deduction for her filing status. What should she do?
Choice1: Itemize anyway, since she has receipts
Choice2: Take the standard deduction, since it produces a better result
Choice3: Average the two amounts
Explanation: Taxpayers should use whichever is larger - the standard deduction or itemized deductions - since either can be used, and the larger one produces a lower taxable income.

Scenario: A taxpayer's unreimbursed medical expenses are below the AGI threshold required before any of it can be deducted. Can any of it be deducted?
Choice1: Yes, the full amount can be deducted regardless of AGI
Choice2: No, only the portion exceeding the AGI threshold on Schedule A is deductible
Choice3: Only if the taxpayer is over 65
Explanation: Medical expenses are deductible only to the extent they exceed a set percentage of the taxpayer's AGI, so amounts below that threshold aren't deductible at all.

Scenario: A taxpayer qualifies for a $1,000 nonrefundable credit but only owes $600 in tax before credits. What happens to the remaining $400?
Choice1: It is refunded to the taxpayer
Choice2: It is generally lost, since a nonrefundable credit can't reduce tax below zero
Choice3: It automatically carries forward to next year in every case
Explanation: A nonrefundable credit can only reduce tax liability to zero - any excess is generally lost unless that specific credit allows a carryforward.

Scenario: A low-income working parent with two qualifying children may be eligible for which refundable credit aimed at working taxpayers?
Choice1: The Lifetime Learning Credit
Choice2: The Earned Income Tax Credit
Choice3: The Foreign Tax Credit
Explanation: The Earned Income Tax Credit is a refundable credit designed to benefit low-to-moderate income working taxpayers, especially those with qualifying children.

Scenario: A taxpayer paid $4,000 in qualified tuition for his child's first year of college. Which credit is designed for exactly this situation?
Choice1: The American Opportunity Credit
Choice2: The Saver's Credit
Choice3: The Child and Dependent Care Credit
Explanation: The American Opportunity Credit is specifically designed for qualified expenses during the first four years of postsecondary education.

Scenario: A married couple files Married Filing Separately. What is a common consequence for their credit eligibility?
Choice1: No change to credit eligibility compared to filing jointly
Choice2: They are disqualified from several major credits, including the Earned Income Tax Credit
Choice3: They automatically qualify for a higher credit rate
Explanation: Married Filing Separately status disqualifies taxpayers from a number of significant credits, including the Earned Income Tax Credit, in most situations.

Scenario: A taxpayer moved from State A to State B halfway through the year and worked in both. What kind of return does State A likely require?
Choice1: A full-year resident return
Choice2: A part-year resident return
Choice3: No return, since he no longer lives there
Explanation: When a taxpayer moves into or out of a state partway through the year, a part-year resident return is typically required for the state they left.

Scenario: A taxpayer lives in State A but works entirely in State B, and the two states have no reciprocity agreement. What generally happens?
Choice1: The taxpayer only files in State A
Choice2: The taxpayer typically files a nonresident return in State B and a resident return in State A, often claiming a credit for taxes paid to State B
Choice3: The taxpayer owes no state tax anywhere
Explanation: Without a reciprocity agreement, income earned in State B is generally taxed there through a nonresident return, while the resident state (State A) usually allows a credit for taxes paid to the other state to avoid double taxation.
